item.title: α2,6-Sialoglycan-regulated antitumor immunity of tumor-infiltrating CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 01 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02299-7

Although hypersialylation on cancer cells and its roles in immune evasion and metastasis are well known, the functional roles of cell-surface sialylation on tumor-infiltrating immune cells (TIICs) are not completely understood. Now an α2,3- or α2,6-sialoglycan linkage-specific barcoding and single-cell RNA sequencing approach reveals differential regulation of α2,3- and α2,6-sialylation in subpopulations of TIICs and correlates sialylation with TIIC phenotypes and functions.

item.title: Adaptive mechanisms and emerging cancer therapeutics for CDK2 inhibitors
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 31 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02307-w

Despite the clinical success of CDK4/6 (cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6) inhibitors, CDK2 remains a challenging therapeutic target. This Perspective highlights emerging cell-cycle insights and novel inhibitor classes, including cyclic peptides and allosteric ligands, that may enable next-generation CDK2 therapies.

item.title: A safety pin against BAX
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02301-2

BAX is a pro-death pore-forming BCL-2 family protein essential for the commitment to apoptotic programmed cell death of mammalian cells under stress. A BAX-selective covalent inhibitor acts as a safety pin, blocking BAX-dependent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and apoptosis.

item.title: An enantioselective covalent inhibitor of BAX confers cytoprotection in vivo
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02297-9

An enantioselective covalent inhibitor was developed that restrains BAX, protecting mouse liver and human motor neurons from injury and establishing covalent BAX inhibition as a promising strategy to block pathological cell death.

item.title: CA-IV-directed small-molecule shuttle enables targeted brain delivery of biologics
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 26 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02294-y

Existing receptor targets to direct delivery of biologics across the blood−brain barrier are ubiquitously expressed in the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral tissues. Now, carbonic anhydrase IV (CA-IV) is identified as a brain-enriched receptor, enabling selective and prolonged delivery of large molecules to the CNS through conjugation of a small molecule targeting CA-IV.

item.title: Topogenic sequence recognition at TIM complexes revealed by a stendomycin-bound structure
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 26 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02304-z

The mitochondrial inner membrane complexes TIM23 and TIM22 mediate distinct protein topogenesis functions in polypeptide import. The authors reveal their mechanistic overlap in topogenic sequence recognition by cryo-EM and functional studies using the yeast system and the stendomycin inhibitor.

item.title: Entering the agentic era of AI in drug discovery
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 19 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02295-x

Agentic AI systems are reshaping drug discovery, and the convergence of agentic AI with laboratory automation is enabling the design of self-driving laboratories that transform the design–make–test–analyze cycle into a closed-loop, adaptive workflow. Here, we discuss these advances and the potential that agentic AI holds for drug discovery.

item.title: A chemigenetic endogenous Ras activity biosensor for live-cell pharmacology
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 19 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02276-0

Here the authors present a biosensor for measuring endogenous Ras in live cells, based on HaloTag and the fluorogenic JF635 dye, and they use it to report location-specific inhibition profiles of distinct Ras pathway drugs.

item.title: Living circuit boards built by printing bacterial transistors
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 17 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02300-3

Electronic circuit boards carry out different operations on the basis of the configuration of their components. Now, equivalent biological circuits are engineered that compute functions on the basis of the spatial arrangement of different bacterial strains printed on a surface.

item.title: Photoproximity labeling of c-Myc reveals SLK as a cancer-specific co-regulator
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 13 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02284-0

A photoproximity-labeling approach maps cancer-specific partners of the c-Myc oncoprotein, revealing that the kinase SLK binds and stabilizes c-Myc, drives tumor growth and offers a new strategy to target this long-‘undruggable’ driver of cancer.

item.title: A dual assault on KRAS
item.description:
Representative article figure (not a graphical abstract)

Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 12 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02283-1

KRAS(Q61) mutant oncoproteins drive cancer through defective GTP hydrolysis. A study now shows that small molecules can restore catalytic activity while simultaneously shifting KRAS toward its inactive state, identifying an unexpected strategy to target previously untreatable KRAS mutants.
